newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine presidential race open to all but one.
newsitem.headline: Philippine presidential race open to all but one.

text.p: The Philippine Supreme Court on Tuesday threw the race to succeed President Fidel Ramos wide open by denying him any hope of running for a second term.

The decision erased fears that the court would decide the constitution could be changed to let Ramos run again, possibly triggering unrest. But it gave rise to a new worry -- whether a suitable replacement exists.

When the Philippines rewrote its constitution 10 years ago, it made clear that after two decades under the dictatorship of Ferdinand Marcos, no president could again stay in office for more than one six-year term.
But a private group this year began crossing the country collecting what it says were five million signatures in a petition to change that clause so that Ramos could stand again in 1998.
The Supreme Court on Tuesday said that it stood by its previous decision to bar the petition.

For local and foreign businessmen, who have watched the Philippine economy finally start to thrive under Ramos, the prospect of his reformed-minded government staying on for another six years had in many ways been welcome.
But their hopes had been tempered by stern warnings that once you started tinkering with the constitution, the country's young democracy could start to unravel.
Opposition leaders immediately claimed the court ruling as a triumph for democracy.

"Send the word to all investors, domestic and foreign: political stability is assured now and in the immediate future," said an ecstatic Miriam Santiago, a contender for next May's polls who narrowly lost to Ramos in 1992.

Santiago, a former judge who likes to call her opponents "fungus face", is among at least a dozen politicians to have already thrown their hats in the ring to become the country's third president since the end of Marcos rule in 1986.
None is a clear front-runner and some are likely to be viewed with distaste by foreign investors.
"With none of the candidates posting any convincing lead over the other, this country will just be deluged by political mayhem," said political analyst Nelson Navarro.
Normally fractious opposition parties may have a hard time joining forces to back a Ramos replacement.
Nevertheless there is talk that four opposition parties will this week link up to select a single candidate.
Among the potential candidates is the vice president and one of the country's most popular politicians, Joseph Estrada.

The former action-film hero, who has kept his 1950s-style Elvis Presley coiffure, has a huge following among the masses but in his current ceremonial role has had no chance to prove any skills as an administrator.

Another contender, though not one expected to be backed by the opposition parties, is Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, a trained economist and daughter of a former president who has teamed up with a popular comedian in what is seen as a potentially winning combination.

Other candidates outside the expected opposition alliance include Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo, who styles himself "Tiger Bobby" in reference to U.S. golfer Tiger Woods and in hopes that the Philippines will at last join the ranks of the Asian "tiger" economies.
The most formidable of all candidates is likely to be the one Ramos himself eventually endorses and behind whom he puts his powerful political machinery.

Ramos, a former general who crushed six coup attempts against his predecessor Corazon Aquino, says he never had any intention of running again and argues that democracy is now so embedded in the country's psyche that it would continue whoever succeeds him.
But few analysts are prepared to wager who will be sleeping in the president's Malacanang Palace in Manila this time next year.
"I won't say anything with finality. Politics in the Philippines do not move in straight lines,' one diplomat said.
